To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
NAA, a marker of neurons in the brain, decreases in the aging hippocampal region.
NAA decreases in the hippocampus of normal aging adults and the decrease in hippocampal N-acetylaspartic acid (NAA) is correlated with the decrease in hippocampus volume.
hippocampal N-acetylaspartates (NAA) levels, but not choline-containing compounds (Cho), decrease significantly with age, while hippocampal volume decreases significantly with age.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the neurochemical basis of memory loss in aging.
understanding the neurobiology of aging and the relationship between neuronal injury and cognitive impairment.
the development of a new approach to the study of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the aging hippocampus loses neurons, which are the basic units of memory.
hippocampal neuron loss occurs during normal aging and that NAA is a more sensitive marker than volume for detecting neuron loss.
the hippocampus undergoes a progressive loss of NAA levels with age, which may be related to the loss of neurons, and this loss is associated with a decrease in volume of the structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NAA levels decrease and volumes shrink in the hippocampus of normal aging subjects.
the hippocampus undergoes age-related changes in NAA levels and volume.
the NAA/Cho and NAA/Creatine ratio decreases with aging.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NAA can be used as an indicator of neuronal damage in the aging brain, which can complement the information from MRI.
the hippocampus is a vulnerable region in the brain that undergoes significant changes with normal aging.
NAA levels in the hippocampus decline with age, which is consistent with the view that normal aging is accompanied by gradual neuronal loss.
